en: He will agree to what you say;
For my sake,
The plane-tree garden in Beijing,
And the golden throne within,
Will surely submit to you.
The khanship of Outer Beijing
He will give you in full.
Restrain this rage of yours;
Let us remain alive.
If you do not let us live,
If you torment our fly-sized lives,
If you kill me, I have no recourse;
Lion Manas, mighty leopard,
You will gain not so much as a fly.
I was renowned; I was a khan.
To the seething Chinese people
I was like the Ala-Too mountains.
For Chyn-Machyn, for Beijing,
I was a warrior who bore the burden.
At the edge of the countless people,
On the ridge of swarming enemies,
I lived in a white dwelling.
Know this, my word to you;
Lion Manas, heed my words.
When you rode out on patrol—
‘When bloodthirsty Manas rides out,
He will slaughter every khan’—
We ourselves had heard the news.
We sent out men skilled in discernment
And had them search for you.
Those discerning men searched but failed;
We ourselves
Brought calamity upon ourselves.
I have much to tell; listen.
My Manas, blessed by Khizir,
In anguish I speak; heed my words.
When we held our white dwellings,
We were warriors who drained the world.
Now we are in your hands,
Wretched captives in your grasp.
The treasure where gold is dug—
I will give you my mine as well.
Kara-Kyr, where tea is gathered—
I will give you that land as well.
I have the city of Tash-Köpürö;
In the lands of Tash-Köpürö
I have villages in their tens of thousands.
I will give you those as well.
On its nearer edge,
Agala Chap and Kyzyl-Kum,
Where hunters go and find delight,
Where none could stay with me without enjoyment,
I have land of precious worth—
I will give you that as well.
Killing me will bring no remedy;
If you put me to death,
My ocean, you will gain nothing.
Though I die, words will remain;
There will be no end to my blood-price.
Born to me, Alööke,
I have exactly sixty sons.
Here is a wonder I can tell;
Hear it, generous Manas.
The youngest of the sixty nobles,
The darling of Khan Alööke, now in bonds,
Has studied wondrous arts;
Those who hear his fame take fright.
From the land of those one-eyed people,
From the lake called Abergen,
From the place called Suuk-Tör,
There is a sixty-headed dragon.
Under that dragon
He has studied six years as of this year;
Those who heard his fame took fright.
Six multitudes of boys went together;
All six multitudes were wiped out;
Six boys came back together.
Of Beijing's forty gates,
They say he opened all forty.
He gathered the discerning judges,
Karykan, the khan of Beijing,
And had them file past.
So many judges saw him, they say;
Many of those who saw
Died with their hearts bursting, they say.
Dust rose wherever he walked;
His voice drove the life out of men.
From the hearth an ember rose;
A mighty one named Kongurbay arose.
He began to show a terrible wrath;
The governors who fought him
He slaughtered, leaving none.
They saw the full force of his fury;
Many of the governors
Died with their hearts bursting.
Once they had seen his valor,
They made him a house upon the upland;
All the Chinese gathered,
And that warrior Kongurbay
They made a powerful khan of the Kalmyks.
His valor rose beyond all bounds.
These days the Chinese
Have the warrior Kongurbay
Guard the borders of their people.
I will agree to what you say;
I will send word to the city,
Summon Kongurbay,
And make him your companion.
I will send word to the governors;
I will spread the news far and wide,
For the day you have shown me today,
I shall join
The faith of the Muslims.
Let me send word to the city.
If you and Kongurbay join forces,
Could an enemy approach your watch?
Could any challenger survive?
Could anyone who grapples with you live?
Could one who challenges you prosper?
If you spare my life now,
Let me send word to Kalcha.
My tiger Manas, to you yourself
Let me give him as a companion.'
Broad-jawed, flat-tongued,
A great orator who never faltered,
Alöökö was a wily one.
Not sparing his bare life,
He kept whetting his words at Manas,
Speaking words of many kinds,
He kept singing out to Manas.
Never sated when he drank blood,
Never sparing those who faced him,
Your slaughterer, champion Manas—
When challenged, could he have his fill of blood?
The rabbit that fell into his hands,
Even if it offered its child,
Would Manas leave it alive?
'My senseless black Chinese,
What should I do with your child?
Before my wretched life dies away,
Let me pass my days beheading foes in battle.
Upon the jabbering Chinese
Let me inflict utter humiliation.
I have seven forefathers to avenge;
Let me take his head with my sword!'
Saying this, great Manas,
Enraged and turning pale,
Your khan Manas paused.
Sitting, thinking and considering,
The leopard prince then
Summoned his old fury.
'If not for this Alöökö,
Would my kinsmen not still be living here?
He wore their soles to dust,
Drove them off in every direction.
They have no village settled on the slopes;
They are like a fire gone out.
There is no knowing where they are.
The babbling Manchu,
I see that God has struck him.
When his resources have run out,
This squealing pig
Offers his child as a gift.
This dog who has been captured,
What should I do with his child?
When I have only just come from Altay,
He is sidling up to me;
Desperately, this fool
Is trying to deceive me.
If I regard Alöökö as kin,
This pig with a black exterior,
Will he not learn my secrets?
The calamity I brought upon him,
Will he not bring it on my own head?
Flooding my home with water,
This Chinese, having learned my secrets,
Will he not utterly destroy me?
If by chance I leave him untouched,
If by chance I do not challenge him,
Will the Chinese not grow arrogant?
Will he not send word to his people?
If by chance I let myself be deceived,
If by chance I settle beside him,
Will he feed me and settle as my neighbor?
This infidel, an enemy from the beginning,
Will he turn white and become my kin?!
To this infidel who is deceiving me,
The warrior hero Alöökö,
Will he not learn my secrets from my outward ways?
If it once enters his mind,
Will he not break into my treasury?
If this infidel settles beside me,
Will he not fill himself on my food?
Will he not slaughter my village,
My people, worn and scattered,
Will he not scatter them all over again?
He has the people of Kakan-Chin;
They have been enemies for so long,
They have a custom of shedding blood.
When I look at Alöökö,
Speaking vague, roundabout words,
The mighty man is deceiving me.
If I now obey his words
And settle beside him,
He will keep singing my song with me,
He will learn my secrets for certain.
After he has learned my secrets,
Will he not send wondrous news?
The swarming mass of Chinese,
Will they not advance upon us one day?
Will they not thrust spears over my head?
Will they not slaughter the lords?
Will they not sing their taunting songs?
Will they not plunder us utterly and return?
Will they not bring disaster upon the hero?
All my Kyrgyz people,
Will they not bind them as spoil?
Can one who spares an enemy prosper?
Uncle Bakay, leopard,
Consider it yourself:
A hero like Alöökö,
Can we leave him alive?'
Zulpukor, fallen from the sky,
That was magnanimous Manas's blade.
The enemy who challenged him,
That was the treasure to spill their blood.
When drawn from its sheath with a shout,
It never went idle without drinking blood.
Unless it had drunk its fill of blood,
It would not enter the sheath when put away.
When drawn from its sheath,
It glowed red, becoming blue flame.
If swung at the right moment,
Its length grew forty fathoms.
Joined steel, cast blade,
Guide of the life held in trust,
Zulpukor, given by your God,
Companion of magnanimous Khan Manas.
The double-edged Zulpukor,
He seized it by the hilt,
Drew it from its sheath.
His eyes blazed fiercely like fire,
His blood-drinking urge truly seized him.
His broad white teeth like doors,
Teeth unlike those of the people,
Now jutted glaringly forth.
Could Manas have his fill of blood?
Enraged Khan Manas,
With Zulpukor in his hand,
At a hero like Alöökö
Now swung it.
When he saw this sword,
Hero Alöökö then,
His eyes went staring helplessly.
His precious head, like a traveler's hut,
Flew away, babbling.
